title: Adhortatio ad artes addiscendas

passages.original: ὁ δ’ ἄνθρωπος οὔτε τινὸς τῶν παρ’ ἐκείνοις ἀμελέτητος, 〈ὃς〉 [ἀλλὰ] καὶ τὴν ὑφαντικὴν ἐμιμήσατο τὰς ἀράχνας καὶ πλάττει καθάπερ αἱ μέλισσαι καὶ τοῦ νεῖν οὐκ ἀνάσκητός ἐστι καίτοι πεζὸς ὤν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν θείων τεχνῶν οὐκ ἀπολείπεται, ζηλῶν μὲν τὴν Ἀσκληπιοῦ τέχνην ἰατρικήν, ζηλῶν δ’ Ἀπόλλωνος αὐτήν τε ταύτην καὶ τὰς ἄλλας ἁπάσας ἃς ἔχει, τοξικὴν μουσικὴν μαντικήν, ἔτι τε τῶν Μουσῶν τὴν ἑκάστης ἰδίαν. οὐδὲ γὰρ γεωμετρίας οὐδ’ ἀστρονομίας ἀφίσταται, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ τῆς γῆς νέρθεν καὶ τὰ ὕπερθε τοῦ οὐρανοῦ κατὰ Πίνδαρον ἐπισκοπεῖ. ἐξεπορίσατο δ’ ὑπὸ φιλοπονίας καὶ τὸ μέγιστον τῶν θείων ἀγαθῶν φιλοσοφίαν. διὰ ταῦτα τοίνυν κἂν 〈εἰ〉 λόγου μέτεστι τοῖς ἄλλοις ζῴοις, κατ’ ἐξοχὴν αὐτῶν [καὶ] ὁ ἄνθρωπος μόνος ὀνομάζεται λογικός.
passages.english: But man is unpractised in none of the things those [animals] have: he imitated the spiders in weaving, and he moulds as the bees do, and he is not untrained in swimming, though he is a land creature. More than that, he does not fall short even of the divine arts: he emulates Asclepius' art of medicine, and he emulates Apollo's, both this same [art] and all the others he possesses, archery, music, prophecy, and further the art proper to each of the Muses. For he does not keep away from geometry or astronomy either, but surveys, as Pindar says, both the things beneath the earth and those above the heaven. And through his love of labour he has also procured the greatest of the divine goods, philosophy. For these reasons, then, even if the other animals have some share in reason, man alone is called rational, by pre-eminence over them.
passages.notes: The editor deletes ἀλλὰ and καὶ and supplies ὃς and εἰ; translated accordingly. The closing phrase may also be taken as "man alone, pre-eminently among them, is called rational."

passages.original: καὶ γὰρ καὶ οὗτοι σπάνει τῶν ἰδίων ἀγαθῶν ἐπὶ τὸ γένος ἥκουσιν, οὐδὲ τοσοῦτον γιγνώσκοντες ὅτι ἡ ἄρα εὐγένεια αὕτη ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνονται τοῖς κατὰ πόλιν νομίσμασιν ἔοικεν, ἃ παρὰ τοῖς θεμένοις ἰσχύοντα παρ’ ἄλλοις ἐστὶ κίβδηλα· — οὐδ’ ηὑγένεια σ’ ἦρεν εἰς ὕψος μέγα; — κακὸν τὸ μὴ ἔχειν· τὸ γένος οὐκ ἔβοσκέ με. καλὸς οὖν, [ἧ] φησὶν ὁ Πλάτων, θησαυρὸς αἱ τῶν πατέρων ἀρεταί· κάλλιον δ’ ἀντιθεῖναι δύνασθαι τὸν τοῦ Σθενέλου λόγον ‘ἡμεῖς τοι πατέρων μέγ’ ἀμείνονες εὐχόμεθ’ εἶναι’. ταύτην γὰρ μόνην ἔχοιμεν ἄν, εἰ δή τίς ἐστιν εὐγενείας χρεία, πρὸς οἰκεῖον παράδειγμα τὸν ζῆλον ἡμῖν γίγνεσθαι·
passages.english: For these people too, from lack of goods of their own, take refuge in their descent, without knowing even this much: that this noble birth on which they pride themselves is like the coinages of cities, which are valid among those who issued them but counterfeit among others. — "Did not your noble birth raise you to a great height?" — "It is a bad thing to have nothing; my descent did not feed me." Fine, then, as Plato says, is the treasure of our fathers' virtues; but finer still to be able to set against it the words of Sthenelus: "We claim, you know, to be far better than our fathers." For this is the only [use] we could have of noble birth, if there is indeed any use for it: that our emulation be roused by an example of our own family.
passages.notes: The quoted exchange appears to be from a tragedy (possibly Euripides); speaker attribution uncertain. The Sthenelus line is Homer, Iliad 4.405.

passages.original: μάθοις δ’ ἂν ἐναργέστατα τὸ τοιοῦτον ἀληθὲς ὄν, εἰ τὸν Ὑπέρβολον ἢ τὸν Κλέωνα λογίσαιο, τοσοῦτον ἀπὸ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν κερδήσαντας ὅσον ἄν τις εἰς περιφάνειαν κακὸς ὢν ἐπικτήσαιτο. ‘ἦν ὅτε σύας Βοιώτιον ἔθνος ἔνεπον’ ὁ Πίνδαρός φησι, καὶ πάλιν ὁ αὐτὸς ‘εἰ φεύγομεν Βοιωτίαν ὗν’, ἀξιῶν ὅλου σχεδὸν ἔθνους τὸν ἐπ’ ἀμαθείᾳ ψόγον ἀπολύεσθαι διὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μουσικήν.
passages.english: You would learn most clearly that this is true if you considered Hyperbolus or Cleon, who gained from Athens just as much as a bad man might acquire by way of notoriety. "There was a time when they called the Boeotian race swine," says Pindar, and again the same poet: "if we escape [the name] 'Boeotian pig'," claiming to free almost a whole nation from the reproach of ignorance through his own poetry.

passages.original: τέχνης 〈γὰρ〉 ἁπάσης κατ’ ἐκεῖνον μάλιστα τὸν χρόνον ἀσκουμένης ἡνίχ’ ὡραιότατα φαίνεται τὰ σώματα, πολλοῖς συνέβη περιβλέπτοις διὰ κάλλος γεγενημένοις ἀμελῆσαι τῆς ἑαυτῶν ψυχῆς, εἶθ’ ὕστερον ὅτ’ οὐδὲν ὄφελος λέγειν ‘εἴθ’ ὤφελεν τὸ κάλλος, ὅ με διώλεσε, κακῶς ὀλέσθαι’. τηνικαῦτα δ’ αὐτοὺς καὶ τὸ τοῦ Σόλωνος εἰσέρχεται σκοπεῖσθαι κελεύοντος ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα τὸ τέλος τοῦ βίου. εἶτα καὶ τῷ γήρᾳ λοιδοροῦνται, δέον ἑαυτοῖς, καὶ τὸν Εὐριπίδην ἐπαινοῦσι λέγοντα οὐκ ἀσφαλὲς εἶναι περαιτέρω τὸ κάλλος ἢ μέσον λαβεῖν. ἄμεινον οὖν ἐστιν ἐγνωκότας τὴν μὲν τῶν μειρακίων ὥραν τοῖς ἠρινοῖς ἄνθεσιν ἐοικυῖαν ὀλιγοχρόνιόν τε τὴν τέρψιν ἔχουσαν ἐπαινεῖν 〈ἐκεῖνόν〉 τε καὶ τὴν Λεσβίαν λέγουσαν ‘ὁ μὲν γὰρ καλὸς ὅσσον ἰδεῖν πέλεται 〈καλός〉, ὁ δὲ κἀγαθὸς αὐτίκα καὶ καλὸς ἔσται’, πείθεσθαι δὲ καὶ Σόλωνι τὴν αὐτὴν γνώμην ἐνδεικνυμένῳ, τὸ δὲ γῆρας καθάπερ χαλεπὸν ἐφεδρεύοντα χειμῶνα, δεόμενον οὐχ ὑποδημάτων μόνον καὶ ἐσθῆτος ἀλλὰ καὶ οἰκήσεως ἐπιτηδείας καὶ μυρίων ἄλλων, παρασκευάζεσθαι πρὸς αὐτὸ καθάπερ ἀγαθὸν κυβερνήτην ἐκ πολλοῦ πρὸς χειμῶνα·
passages.english: For since every art is practised above all at that time of life when bodies appear most in their bloom, it has happened to many who became conspicuous for their beauty that they neglected their own soul, and then later, when it was of no use, they said: "Would that the beauty which has destroyed me had perished miserably!" At that point there also comes into their minds the saying of Solon, who bids us consider above all the end of life. Then they even revile old age, when they ought [to revile] themselves, and they praise Euripides when he says that it is not safe to have beauty beyond the middle measure. It is better, then, recognising that the bloom of youths is like spring flowers and has a short-lived delight, to praise him and also the Lesbian woman who says, "For he who is beautiful is beautiful as far as the eye sees, but he who is also good will at once be beautiful too," and to obey Solon, who expresses the same opinion; and, as for old age, lying in wait like a harsh winter and needing not only shoes and clothing but also suitable housing and countless other things, to prepare for it, as a good helmsman [prepares] long beforehand for a storm.
passages.notes: "Him" (ἐκεῖνον, supplied by the editor) presumably refers back to Euripides. The Lesbian woman is Sappho.

passages.original: Ἀσκληπιός γέ τοι καὶ Διόνυσος, εἴτ’ ἄνθρωποι πρότερον ἤστην εἴτ’ ἀρχῆθεν θεοί, τιμῶν ἀξιοῦνται μεγίστων, ὃ μὲν διὰ τὴν ἰατρικήν, ὃ δ’ ὅτι τὴν περὶ τὰς ἀμπέλους ἠμᾶς τέχνην ἐδίδαξεν. εἰ δ’ οὐκ ἐθέλεις ἐμοὶ πείθεσθαι, τόν γε θεὸν αἰδέσθητι τὸν Πύθιον· οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ καὶ τὸν Σωκράτην εἰπὼν ἀνδρῶν ἁπάντων σοφώτατον εἶναι, καὶ τῷ Λυκούργῳ προσφωνήσας ὧδ’ εἶπεν·
passages.english: Asclepius, at any rate, and Dionysus, whether they were formerly men or gods from the beginning, are deemed worthy of the greatest honours, the one on account of medicine, the other because he taught us the art concerning vines. But if you are not willing to believe me, at least show reverence to the Pythian god. He is the one who both declared Socrates to be the wisest of all men and, addressing Lycurgus, spoke thus:
passages.notes: ἠμᾶς is evidently a misprint for ἡμᾶς ("us"). The passage ends with a colon introducing the oracle to Lycurgus, which is quoted in the following text (not given here). "The Pythian god" is Apollo of Delphi.

passages.original: πότερον οὖν Εὐριπίδου μὲν καὶ τῶν τοιούτων καταγνῶμεν, τοῖς δὲ φιλοσόφοις ἐπιτρέψωμεν τὴν κρίσιν; ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τούτων ἁπάντων ὥσπερ ἐξ ἑνὸς στόματος ὡμολόγηται φαῦλον εἶναι τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα. οὐδὲ μὴν οὐδὲ τῶν ἰατρῶν τις ἐπῄνεσεν αὐτό· πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ Ἱπποκράτους ἀκούσῃ λέγοντος ‘διάθεσις ἀθλητικὴ οὐ φύσεις, ἕξις ὑγιεινὴ κρείσσων’, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων τῶν μετ’ αὐτὸν ἀρίστων ἰατρῶν. ὅλως μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ μάρτυρος οὐκ ἐβουλόμην κρίνεσθαι· ῥητορικὸν γὰρ τὸ τοιοῦτον μᾶλλον ἢ τιμῶντος ἀλήθειαν ἀνδρός· ὅμως δ’ ἐπειδή τινες ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον καταφεύγουσι καὶ τὴν παρὰ τούτων κενὴν δόξαν, ἀφέντες αὐτὸ 〈τὸ〉 ἐπιτήδευμα γυμνὸν τῶν ἔξωθεν σκοπεῖν, ἠναγκάσθην κἀγὼ τούτους προχειρίσασθαι τοὺς μάρτυρας, ἵν’ ὅτι μηδ’ ἐνταῦθα πλέον ἔχουσί τι γιγνώσκωσιν.
passages.english: Shall we, then, condemn Euripides and men like him, and entrust the judgement to the philosophers? But by all of these too, as if from one mouth, it is agreed that the pursuit is worthless. Nor indeed has any of the physicians praised it: first you will hear Hippocrates saying, "The athletic condition is not natural; a healthy state is better," and then all the other best physicians after him. Now I did not wish at all to have the matter decided by witnesses; for such a thing belongs rather to a rhetorician than to a man who honours truth. Yet since some take refuge in the praise of the many and the empty reputation they get from them, having given up examining the pursuit itself stripped of externals, I too was compelled to bring forward these witnesses, so that they may know that even here they have no advantage.
passages.notes: "The pursuit" is athletics, the subject of the surrounding argument. The Hippocratic text ‘διάθεσις ἀθλητικὴ οὐ φύσεις’ is likely corrupt; translated as "not natural".

passages.original: ποίας, ὦ πρὸς θεῶν, ἰσχύος καὶ ποῦ χρησίμης; πότερον τῆς εἰς τὰ γεωργικὰ τῶν ἔργων; πάνυ μὲν οὖν καλῶς ἢ σκάπτειν ἢ θερίζειν ἢ ἀροῦν 〈ἤ〉 τι τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ γεωργίαν δύνανται. ἀλλ’ ἴσως 〈τῆς〉 εἰς τὰ πολεμικά; τὸν Εὐριπίδην αὖθίς μοι κάλει, ὅστις αὐτοὺς ὑμνήσει λέγων ‘πότερα μαχοῦνται πολεμίοισιν, ἐν χεροῖν δίσκους ἔχοντες;’ τῷ γὰρ ὄντι ‘οὐδεὶς σιδήρου ταῦτα μωραίνει πέλας’. ἀλλὰ πρὸς κρύος καὶ θάλπος ἰσχυροί; αὐτοῦ γε τοῦ Ἡρακλέους ζηλωταί, ὡς ἑνὶ καὶ χειμῶνι καὶ θέρει σκέπεσθαι δέρματι, ὡς ἀνυπόδετοι διατελεῖν, ὑπαίθριοι κοιμᾶσθαι, χαμευνεῖν·
passages.english: Strength of what kind, by the gods, and useful where? For farm work? Very well indeed, then, they are able to dig or reap or plough or do any of the other tasks of farming! But perhaps for war? Call Euripides for me again, who will hymn them, saying: "Will they fight the enemy holding discuses in their hands?" For in truth, "nobody plays these fool's games near the iron." But are they strong against cold and heat? Emulators of Heracles himself, no doubt, so as to be covered by a single hide in winter and summer, to go on unshod, to sleep in the open, to lie on the ground!
passages.notes: The questions and the remark on farming are ironic.
